title: City of Las Cruce's Motion for Order Compelling El Paso Electric Company Discovery Responses and Tolling Testimony Deadlines  [Motion]

documents.name: DOC-000379834-26
documents.text:
BEFORE THE NEW MEXICO PUBLIC REGULATION COMMISSION

IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF EL PASO                        )
ELECTRIC COMPANY FOR REVISION OF ITS RETAIL                        )   Docket No. 25-00082-UT
ELECTRIC RATES PURSUANT TO ADVICE NOTICE                           )
NO. 317                                                            )

     THE CITY OF LAS CRUCES’ MOTION FOR AN ORDER COMPELLING
   EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY TO PROVIDE RESPONSES TO DISCOVERY
   REQUESTS AND TOLLING THE PROCEDURAL ORDER’S DEADLINES FOR
 INTERVENOR AND STAFF DIRECT TESTIMONY AND REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

       COMES NOW the City of Las Cruces (the “City” or “CLC”), by and through the

undersigned attorneys, and pursuant to 1.2.2.25(J) NMAC and 1.2.2.12(C)(1)(e) NMAC, moves

the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (the “NMPRC” or “Commission”) compelling

El Paso Electric Company’s (“Company” or “EPE”) to provide responses to discovery requests

propounded by the City nearly one month ago, which EPE has failed to answer despite numerous

requests by the City. The City also asks the Commission to modify the Procedural Order issued

on , and to toll the deadlines of July 24, 2026, for direct testimony by intervenors and Staff and

August 19, 2026, for rebuttal testimony for periods commensurate with EPE’s delay in providing

discovery responses.

       As grounds for this motion, the City states:

       1.      After requesting and receiving an order from the Commission granting it a variance

from the requirement that a general rate case be filed no later than 150 days from the end of the

Base Period, EPE filed its 4,157-page Application for Revision of Retail Electric Rates

(“Application”) on March 27, 2026. See EPE’s Unopposed and Verified Motion for Variance

Regarding Rate Case Filing Deadline (Feb. 6, 2026); Order Granting Extension of Time (Feb. 19,

2026); EPE’s Application for Revision of Retail Electric Rates (Mar. 27, 2026).

       2.      On April 15, 2026, the day before the scheduled prehearing conference, EPE filed

a 1,657-page Notice of Errata and Filing of Replacement Exhibits, which consisted of corrections
 to the testimony of two of the Company’s witnesses, a replacement Schedule A-3, and the

workpapers for several of its filed schedules. See Notice of Errata and Filing of Replacement

Exhibits (Apr. 15, 2026); see also Order Setting Prehearing Conference (Apr. 3, 2026).

       3.      On April 24, 2026, the Commission issued an Order Suspending Advice Notice No.

317, in which it determined that EPE’s Application was deemed complete as of April 15, 2026,

and that the statutory period for suspension of the Company’s proposed rates should begin 30 days

thereafter and continue for an initial period of nine months. See Order Suspending Advice Notice

No. 317, ¶¶ 15-18 (dated Apr. 23, 2026 and filed Apr. 24, 2026).

       4.      On April 27, 2026, the Hearing Examiners issued a Procedural Order that, among

other things, set deadlines based on the nine-month suspension period and encouraged parties to

reach agreements regarding discovery matters. See Procedural Order, ¶¶ A, E-K. That order

provides that Staff and intervenor direct testimony shall be filed by July 24, 2026; rebutally

testimony shall be filed by August 19, 2026; and an evidentiary hearing will begin on September

21, 2026. See id. at ¶¶ G, I, K.

       5.      The City moved to intervene in this proceeding on April 27, 2026. See City’s

Motion for Leave to Intervene, Request to Modify the Service List, and Request for Discovery

Requests and Responses (Apr. 27, 2026).

       6.      On May 21, 2026, the City served its first set of discovery requests on EPE, in the

form solely of requests for production of documents. See City’s First Set of Requests for

Production of Documents (May 21, 2026) (attached as Exhibit 1.) The City served its second set

of discovery requests on EPE on May 26, 2026, also in the form of requests for production of

documents. See City’s Second Set of Requests for Production of Documents (May 26, 2026)

(attached as Exhibit 2.) Subsequently, the City has served EPE with seven sets of interrogatories

and requests for production of documents, as well as two joint sets of discovery requests from the

                                                2
 City and Doña Ana County. Those subsequent discovery requests are not the subject of this motion

to compel EPE to respond to the City’s discovery requests, but the City hopes that the Commission

will establish standards in ruling upon this motion that minimize future discovery disputes.

        7.     On Friday, June 5, 2026, at or about 4:21 p.m., EPE emailed its objections to the

City’s First Set of Requests for Production of Documents to the City and other parties and

separately emailed links to its Box cloud-based file sharing platform for non-confidential and

confidential responses. See Exhibit 3, June 5, 2026 email messages.

        8.     On Monday, June 8, 2026, after beginning to review EPE’s objections and

responses, counsel for the City sent an email message to EPE’s counsel noting that it was not

proper for EPE to respond to requests for production of documents, for example several of the first

requests for production, by stating that “EPE will produce responsive documents . . . once they are

identified.” See Exhibit 4, Email Message from A. Stevens to J. Wechsler et al. dated June 8,

2026.   Under Rule 1.2.2.25(F)(5) NMAC, the party receiving a request for production of

documents has 15 days in which either to object or to “produce as requested all documents or

things which are not the subject of an objection.” Moreover, if the party receiving a request for

production of documents needs more time, it that party’s duty to seek agreement about a different

time frame before the deadline. See 1.2.2.25(F)(4) NMAC.

        9.     In that June 8, 2026, email message to EPE counsel, the City’s counsel also

complied with EPE’s request for a signed FERC confidentiality agreement before the Company

would produce copies of FERC “cluster studies” or periodic system upgrade studies. See Ex. 3;

see also Exhibit 5, EPE’s Responses to City’s First Set of Requests for Production of Documents,

at Response to Request for Production CLC 1-5; Exhibit 6, EPE’s Objections and Responses to

the City’s First Set of Discovery Requests.



                                                3
        10.     A week later, having received no response from EPE’s counsel and no supplemental

discovery responses, counsel for the City sent another email message to EPE’s counsel specifying

the reasons why 24 of EPE’s responses to 38 requests for production of documents were non-

responsive and noting that no supplemental responses had been provided in the several instances

in which EPE vaguely had stated that it would produce responsive documents when they were

located. See Exhibit 7, Email Message from A. Stevens to J. Wechsler et al. dated June 15, 2026.

        11.    Less than an hour after the City’s second email message was sent, EPE attorney

Kari Olson telephoned City attorney Anastasia Stevens. Their discussion touched upon Requests

for Production CLC 1-1 through 1-5, which had been the subject of the City’s first email message

on June 8 and which had been repeated in the City’s June 15 email message. Ms. Olson told Ms.

Stevens that the City’s requests for “correspondence” had generated a huge number of answers

when EPE searched its email files, and that EPE would have to thin the results down and produce

a privilege log. To date, no email messages or any other correspondence has been produced, with

or without a privilege log.

       12.     During that June 15, 2026, telephone conference, Ms. Stevens and Ms. Olson also

discussed Request for Production CLC 1-38, which requested that EPE produce its daily “Costing

Model” from April 2023 through March 2026. Ms. Stevens explained that the time frame was

chosen to coincide with EPE’s participation in the Western Energy Imbalance Market (“WEIM”).

They agreed that EPE would first produce daily Costing Models for June through September 2025,

although maybe the City would want more. They also agreed that Ms. Stevens would confer with

her consultant to ascertain what portions of the FERC cluster studies were needed.

       13.     Two days later, on June 17, 2026, counsel for the City sent an email message to

EPE counsel Olson, cc to EPE’s other counsel, stating that in response to Request for Production

CLC 1-38, the City would need Costing Models for the entire base period of October 1, 2024,

                                               4
 through September 30, 2025, i.e., one-third of its original request. See Exhibit 8, Email Message

from A. Stevens to K. Olson et al. dated June 17, 2026. That email message reiterated and clarified

the City’s expectations regarding responses to seven more of the unsatisfactory responses that had

been described in the City’s June 15, 2026 email message, emphasizing that producing video and

audio of EPE’s advertising in response to Request for Production CLC 1-23 probably would take

some time. See id.; see also Ex. 6. It also advised EPE that the City’s consultant had not yet

provided specifications regarding the FERC cluster studies. See Ex. 7.

       14.     On Friday, June 19, 2026, counsel for the City sent an email message to counsel for

EPE concerning the Company’s apparent misinterpretation of Request for Production CLC-2-8.

See Exhibit 9, Email Message from A. Stevens to J. Wechsler, K. Olson, et al. dated June 19, 2026;

see also Exhibit 10, EPE’s Responses to City’s Second Set of Discovery Requests, Response to

Request for Production CLC 2-8. The message explained that the City was seeking engineering

studies and budget documents related to the planned outage of Newman Unit 3 in 2023, which

effectively was superseded by an unplanned outage about which EPE had provided responses and

documentation in response to Request for Production CLC 2-5 and Staff Interrogatory/Request for

Production 1-31. See id. It asked for documents and engineering support for the “original” budget

about which EPE witness Jeffery Hughes testified. See id.

       15.     On Monday, June 22, 2026, counsel for the City sent an email message to counsel

for EPE about the Company’s response to Request for Production CLC 2-18 merely stating that

EPE was in the process of evaluating and responding to CLC 2-18 and would “supplement this

response once the evaluation was complete.” See Exhibit 11, Email Message from A. Stevens to

K. Olson, J. Wechsler, et al. dated June 22, 2026; see also Ex. 10 at EPE’s Response to CLC 2-

18.



                                                5
        16.     On the evening of Monday, June 22, 2026, EPE attorney Jeff Wechsler sent an

email message to counsel for the City stating that he had set aside time the next day to go through

the discovery issues raised by the City and hoped to provide an answer to the City’s email messages

at that time. See Exhibit 12, Email Message from J. Wechsler to A. Stevens, et al. dated June 22,

2026. Mr. Wechsler also stated that “EPE will continue to work in good faith to provide

meaningful responses in discovery, including by providing supplemental responses when

appropriate.” See id. However, he stated that “EPE is not amenable to an extension of the current

deadlines,” as the City’s previous email messages had suggested. See id.; see also, e.g. Ex. 7, 11.

       17.    On the evening of Thursday, June 25, 2026, EPE attorney Wechsler emailed a letter

to counsel for the City. See Exhibit 13, Email Message from J. Wechsler to A. Stevens, et al. dated

June 25, 2026. Mr. Wechsler said he would be out of the office on Friday but would be available

for discussion early the following week. See id.

       18.     EPE’s letter, which is dated June 24, 2026, but was emailed to counsel for the City

at 6:49 p.m. on June 25, 2026, does address, item by item, the concerns raised in the City’s five

email messages to EPE’s counsel. See Exhibit 13, Letter from J. Wechsler to A. Stevens dated

June 24, 2026; compare id. with Ex. 4, 7, 8, 9, 11. However, EPE does not fully commit to

providing supplemental responses and its tentative statements about supplementing its responses

mostly identify July 10 as the target date, with some on July 2, July 3, and as late as July 17, which

is exactly one week before intervenor and Staff direct testimony is due. See Ex. 13, CLC Issue

Nos. 3 (CLC 1-2), 6 (CLC 1-5), 13 (CLC 1-19(d)), 17 (CLC 1-23), 18 (CLC 1-27), 24 (CLC 1-

38), 25 (CLC 2-8), 26 (CLC 2-18).

       19.      While these potential document production dates are at least 27 days after EPE

was required to respond to the City’s discovery requests—and as much as 42 days late—it should

be noted that EPE already has failed to meet its first self-granted extension of time. Request for

                                                   6
 Production CLC 2-18 referred to Exhibit SAS-1 of the Direct Testimony of Steven A. Sierra and

Workpaper A-03 for the Total Company and the New Mexico jurisdiction and asked EPE to

provide “(a) itemized general ledger entries and invoices that support each amount shown as

Outside Services Employed during the base period, as well as for EPE’s proposed adjustments, if

any; and (b) EPE’s calculations supporting the jurisdictional cost allocation factors proposed in

this proceeding for FERC Account 923 Outside Services Employed.” See Ex. 2, Request for

Production CLC 2-18. EPE’s response stated that “Discovery is ongoing. EPE is in the process

of evaluating and responding to CLC 2-18. EPE will supplement this response once the evaluation

is complete.” Although EPE has provided general ledger entries and invoices in response to a

number of discovery requests by the City, Staff and other parties, did not answer this request by

the deadline of June 10, 2026, under 1.2.2.25 NMAC and did not provide an answer by July 2,

2026, as it said it would.

       20.      EPE’s failure to meet its first self-imposed extended deadline does not give the

City any hope that it will produce any other supplemental discovery responses absent an order

from the Commission directing it to do so by a date or dates certain.

       21.     Although for the most part the City will address EPE’s inadequate discovery

responses in the order set forth in Mr. Wechsler’s letter, it is appropriate to begin with Request

for Production CLC 1-38, which is labeled CLC Issue No. 23 in that letter. See also id. at CLC

Issue No. 24. As explained above in Paragraphs 12 and 13, Request for Production CLC 1-38

asked EPE to produce copies of its Costing Model from April 2023 through March 2026. The

Costing Model, which EPE has produced in discovery in a number of previous Commission

dockets, contains a wealth of information on an hourly basis about EPE’s total system load, the

generation output of individual EPE-owned local gas generation units, the generation from EPE’s

total share of the Palo Verde Nuclear Generation Station (“PVNGS”), and the combined output of

                                                7
 all of its renewable energy resources. It also includes information about hourly energy sales and

purchases by EPE, pricing, and availability of the generating units that EPE owns. While there

are some shortcomings—the load data is on a total company basis and the renewable energy

resources are reported as a single agglomerated reduction to load—experience has shown that the

Costing Models are excellent sources of detailed historical data about EPE’s operations.

       22.     As indicated above in Paragraphs 12 and 13, the City first asked for three years of

daily costing models. During a conversation with EPE counsel Kari Olson, counsel for the City

agreed that the months of June 2025 through September 2025—the summer peak period during

the base period for this rate case—were the most important. A few days later, counsel for the City

emailed counsel for EPE asking for the Costing Models for the entire base period, but not three

years. Inexplicably, Mr. Wechsler’s letter has condensed the City’s request to just three months,

July through September 2026. See Exhibit 13, Wechsler Letter, at CLC Issue No. 24.

       23.     Not only has EPE shrunken the City’s request for Costing Models from three years

to three months. The letter states that EPE will supplement CLC 1-38, i.e., provide any response

at all, by July 17, 2026. See id. Staff and intervenor direct testimony currently is due to be filed

by July 24, 2026. See Procedural Order, ¶ G. It would be virtually impossible to digest the

information in the Costing Models and to incorporate them into the City’s analysis and then into

the form of prefiled direct testimony and exhibits in the span of a week.

       24.     The importance of the hourly historical data available in the Costing Model cannot

be overstated. The City recently filed a Motion to Dismiss EPE’s Application on the grounds that

the Company’s rate application mixes elements of a historical test year period filing with elements

of a future test year filing and does not provide the linkage data to connect historical data with

projected future figures. See City’s Motion to Dismiss EPE’s Application (submitted June 29,

2026 and accepted for filing on June 30, 2026). The City recognized early in its evaluation of

                                                 8
 EPE’s Application that a significant portion of the requested base rate increase of more than 50

percent was attributable to interjurisdictional cost allocations that had unexpectedly increased from

EPE’s last general rate proceeding, NMPRC Case No. 20-00104-UT, despite the Company’s

procurement of considerable amounts of New Mexico-dedicated renewable energy resources in

the interim to satisfy a increasing statutory Renewable Portfolio Standard requirements. The City

decided that, in the absence of support by EPE for its proposed interjurisdictional cost allocation

factors, it would attempt to evaluate the actual contributions of dedicated resources in order to

develop alternative allocation factors. The Costing Models that the City sought would provide a

considerable amount of the historical information that the City needs to perform this analysis.

       25.     In short, EPE’s withholding of the Costing Models for the base period has stymied

the City’s development and presentation of its position, almost totally. EPE must understand that;

the City has not hidden its intentions. It is hardly surprising, therefore, that EPE would withhold

the information that is essential to the City’s case. Indeed, EPE’s offer to provide a fraction of the

requested information a week before the City’s direct testimony is due is a blatant affront to the

City and to the rate case litigation process.

       26.     While EPE’s withholding of other responsive documents is not quite as devastating

as its position on the Costing Model, the Company’s positions are not tenable under the law and a

common-sense approach to this docket. They will be addressed consectively, for ease of reference.

       27.     Request for Production CLC 1-1 asked EPE to produce copies of any agreements

that EPE has entered into with potential large load customers as that term is used in proposed Rate

Nos. 50 and 51, regardless of whether the potential large load customer was located in EPE’s New

Mexico or Texas service area. See Ex. 1, Request for Production CLC 1-1. EPE objected on the

grounds that the request was vague and irrelevant but produced a copy of its executed agreement

with Borderplex Digital Verde, LLC confidentially, stating that was the only potential large load

                                                  9
 customer with an agreement that would potentially take service in New Mexico under Rates 50

and 51. See Ex. 5 at EPE’s Response to CLC 1-1; see also Ex. 6 at EPE’s Objections to CLC 1-1.

The City interpreted EPE’s object as claiming that its tariffs and agreements in the Texas

jurisdiction are not relevant to the issues in this case and could not lead to the discovery of

admissible evidence. See Ex. 7, Item CLC 1-1; see also 1-026(B)(1) NMRA.

       28.     Knowing that EPE’s large load tariffs approved by the Public Utility Commission

of Texas (“PUCT”) are similar to those proposed in this New Mexico docket, the City asserted

that “[w]hether EPE has negotiated similar or different terms in its Texas jurisdiction as it is

proposing similar large load tariffs in NM is quite relevant to evaluating the NM proposal.” See

Ex. 7, Item CLC 1-1. Obviously, it is relevant for the Commission and the parties to know whether

the Company has negotiated agreements with more or less rigorous protections for itself and

existing ratepayers in one or the other jurisdiction, even if the actual agreement in the Texas

jurisdiction were not admissible in this case. See 1-026(B)(1) NMRA. Likewise, it would be

relevant if agreements that EPE has entered into with potential large load customers were to reveal

that the same data center developers were playing off one jurisdiction against the other to obtain

better terms. Mr. Wechsler’s assertion that he fails to see how responsive documents would be

likely to lead to admissible evidence in the present case demonstrates a lack of creativity as well

as the Company’s resistance to produce documents that certainly might lead to admissible cross-

examination of EPE’s witnesses, if not actual admission of the full agreements from Texas.

       29.     Request for Production CLC 1-2 asked EPE to produce all correspondence,

internal or internal, relating to the agreements produced in response to CLC 1-1. See Ex. 1 at CLC

1-2. EPE objected on the grounds that the request sought privileged information and commercially

sensitive information and was overly broad. See Ex. 6 at CLC 1-2. The Company then responded

that “EPE will produce responsive documents ‘relating to the agreements’ between EPE and ‘large

                                                10
 load customers’ once they are identified.” See Ex. 5 at CLC 1-2. EPE did not say when it would

do that.

        30.       EPE’s Response to Request for Production CLC 1-2 reveals a flaw that runs

throughout the Company’s discovery responses and objections. If a recipient of discovery

responses needs more time to answer discovery, the request for more time should be made to the

proponent of the discovery before the deadline, not at the time that responses are due. See

1.2.2.25(F)(5) NMAC. In other words, it is not a proper objection to say that we will get to your

request when we get to it; unless there is a valid objection to any production, responsive documents

must be produced within the 15-day period allowed. See id.

           31. The City’s June 15, 2026 email message to EPE’s counsel noted that three and one-

half weeks already had elapsed with no responsive documents produced.              See Ex. 7. Mr.

Wechsler’s letter states that per the telephone discussion between EPE attorney Olson and counsel

for the City, EPE was still in the process of searching across the company for such correspondence

and anticipated having a supplemental response by July 3, 2026. See Ex. 14 at CLC Issue No. 3.

As of the filing of this motion, that has not occurred.

        32.       Request for Production CLC 1-3 asked for correspondence relating to potential

large load customers regardless of whether agreements had been reached and regardless of whether

they were in the New Mexico or Texas jurisdiction. See Ex. 1 at CLC 1-3. Somewhat conversely

Request for Production CLC 1-4 asked for all agreements and correspondence relating to the

potential large load customer with a load of 80 MW mentioned in the Direct Testimony of EPE

witness James Schichtl. See Ex. 1 at CLC 1-4. EPE objected on the grounds that both these

requests were duplicative of previously requested documents. See Ex. 6 at CLC 1-3, CLC 1-4.

However, EPE also responded that responsive documents either have been or will be provided in

response to Requests for Production CLC 1-1 or CLC 1-2. See Ex. 5 at CLC 1-3, CLC 1-4. EPE’s

                                                 11
 pattern of delayed responses is repeated in Mr. Wechsler’s Letter, which may or may not indicate

that the Company anticipates having a supplemental response by July 3, 2026, which is (i) a legal

holiday and (ii) four weeks after the responses were due. See Ex. 14 at CLC Issue Nos. 4 & 5.

       33.     EPE’s position on Request for Production CLC 1-5 as stated in the Wechsler Letter

is acceptable to the City for the time being, especially if the referenced supplemental response to

Staff 5-1 is truly responsive. See id. at CLC Issue No. 6.

       34.     Request for Production CLC 1-9 asked for copies of EPE’s Distribution

Expansion Plans going back to 2010, and Request for Production CLC 1-10 asked for copies of

EPE’s System Expansion Plans, which address transmission system improvements, going back to

2010. See Ex. 1 at CLC 1-9, CLC 1-10. EPE objected to these requests on the grounds that the

time frame sought was not reasonably limited in scope. See Ex. 6 at CLC 1-9, CLC 1-10. EPE

responded by providing the respective plans going back to 2020. See Ex. 5 at CLC 1-9, CLC 1-

10. The June 17, 2026 email message from counsel to the City to counsel for EPE pointed out that

each distribution and transmission expansion plan covers a ten-year period, so that some if not

many of projects presented in the pre-2020 plans sought by the City would have been completed

and presented by EPE as additions to rate base in this proceeding, not in Case No. 20-00104-UT.

See Ex. 8. Despite that clarification, Mr. Wechsler’s Letter asks, somewhat rhetorically, “Can you

please help me understand how your think a distribution expansion plan [or a system expansion

plan] from 2010 might lead to admissible evidence in this case?” Ex. 14 at CLC Issues Nos. 7, 8.

       35.     It is unlikely that EPE is ready to withdraw its request to increase its rate base in

this case by adding distribution and transmission system additions that were planned between 2010

and 2019 but were completed on and after January 1, 2020. The Company’s opposition to

producing this evidence relating to a substantial portion of its proposed additions to rate base is

difficult to understand and ultimately is untenable.

                                                12
        36.      Request for Production CLC 1-13 requested “copies of documents that record

EPE’s hourly system-wide and New Mexico jurisdictional peak loads for each hour from January

1, 2020 through December 31, 2025.” See Ex. 1 at CLC 1-13. EPE objected on the ground CLC

1-13 “requests information in a form that is not kept by EPE and data that would take many hours

to collect, and EPE objects to the request to the extent it seeks or would require EPE to either

conduct studies or create information not readily available or in EPE’s possession in the form

requested.” See Ex. 6 at CLC 1-13. EPE then responded by providing a document showing hourly

system wide native load and asserting that “EPE does not have hourly peak loads for New

Mexico.” Ex. 5 at CLC 1-13.

       37.      In its June 17, 2026 email message, the City took issue with EPE’s failure to

provide source documents for the system-wide peak loads, as opposed to a tabulation. See Ex. 8.

The City also challenged EPE’s claim that it does not have New Mexico jurisdictional peak loads,

noting that Schedules P-1(a) and P-1(b) state the New Mexico jurisdictional peak load for the peak

hour of each month during the base period. See id. Mr. Wechsler’s Letter first asserts that “EPE

produced a significant amount of information in response to CLC 1-13,” which was about system-

wide peak loads not New Mexico jurisdictional peak loads. He adds that the “specific information

that you identify above—“hourly peak loads for the NM jurisdiction”—is not available in the

format that you have identified.” See Ex. 14 at CLC Issue No. 9.

       38.      However, the City’s Request for Production CLC 1-13 did not ask for any

particular format but simply asked for “documents that record” the hourly New Mexico load. See

Ex. 1 at CLC 1-13. The City’s discovery requests define “document” broadly to included

electronically recorded information. See id. at Definitions ¶ 6. EPE has yet to explain how it was

able to include in its rate case filing Schedules P-1(a) and P-1(b), which state New Mexico

jurisdictional and even New Mexico rate class peak or coincident load values for the peak months

                                               13
 of the base period, without recording peak hourly loads. It seems self-evident that the Company

cannot know which hour of any given month will represent its peak load or maximum coincident

peak load until the end of the month. Therefore, it must have, or at some point have had, peak

load information for hours throughout the month. As indicated above, the City needs historical

data about New Mexico jurisdictional peak loads to develop its position on appropriate

interjurisdiction cost allocation factors in this case.

              39.         Request for Production CLC 1-14 referred to EPE’s response to

Interrogatory and Request for Production Staff 1-29, and asked EPE to “provide the calculations

that resulted in the ‘Peak Contribution (MW)’ values stated for the Buena Vista 1, Santa Teresa,

and Carne battery energy storage systems (“BESS”) stated in that response,” and to “provide any

alternative calculations of the capacity contributions of each of those facilities that EPE has

performed or has had others perform.” Ex. 1 at CLC 1-14. EPE did not assert a specific objection

to this discovery request. See Ex. 6. However, instead of providing the requested calculations,

EPE provided a verbal response to the request for production of documents, as follows:

        The Peak Contribution (MW) is calculated by multiplying the Installed Capacity
        (MW) by the ELCC rating. The ELCC method is used to assign capacity
        contribution toward reliability for each resource type and is an industry established
        metric appropriate for measuring resource adequacy contribution toward reliability.
        EPE does not assume alternative calculations for capacity contribution.

Ex. 5 at CLC 1-14.

        40.         In its June 17 email message, the City repeated its request for calculations. See Ex.

8. On June 25, 2026, EPE sent a letter to counsel for the City stating that “[w]e will investigate

how the ‘Peak Contribution’ column was determined in Staff 1-29. If there are calculations that

are responsive to your request, EPE will supplement its response as soon as possible.” Ex. 14 at

CLC Issue No. 10. Of course there are calculations; EPE’s response quoted above describes one



                                                     14
 step in the calculations. What the City requested—and still has not received from EPE—are the

calculations under the ELCC methodology.

       41.     Request for Production CLC 1-15 asked for documentation of energy production,

battery storage charging status, battery storage discharge, and deliveries of energy from the Buena

Vista solar facility directly to EPE’s system on an hourly basis, or on 30-minute, 15-minute or any

other smaller interval basis reported to or recorded by EPE since that facility began producing

energy. See Ex. 1 at CLC 1-15. EPE objected on the grounds that the request was “vague and

ambiguous, including the phrases ‘battery storage charging status’ and ‘battery storage charge

level.’” See Ex. 6 at CLC 1-15.

       42.     Nevertheless, EPE produced a document titled CLC 01-15_Attachment 01, stating

that it shows “the 5-minute interval net generation output for Buena Vista 1 BESS for the

timeframe requested.” See Ex. 5 at CLC 1-15. A page of that 7,053 page document was included

in the City’s Motion to Dismiss EPE’s Application as Exhibit C and is attached hereto as Exhibit

15. That rather obscure printout does not fully address the City’s Request for Production CLC 1-

15, which also asked for energy production from Buena Vista 1 and deliveries of energy from

Buena Vista 1 directly to EPE’s system. Compare Ex. 15 with Ex. 1 at CLC 1-15. The City

expressed these points in its June 17, 2026 email message to EPE’s counsel. See Ex. 8.

       43.     However, the Wechsler Letter claims that the request is “vague and ambiguous
